titleEn: Happy are those whose way is blameless
progression: | Am Am | Em Em | Am Dm | Em Am |
intro: The longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses on one subject, and an alphabetical acrostic built to be recited in pieces rather than read straight through. That is how the widespread custom works of saying the stanzas that spell a person's name at a grave or on a yahrzeit. For a learner it is the best vocabulary drill in the book: eight nouns and a short list of imperatives come back verse after verse, so the fiftieth verse costs a fraction of the first. Start with the nun stanza and its best known line, {{105.2}}, a lamp for my feet.

stichs.en: Happy are those blameless of way,
who walk in the teaching of the LORD.

verses.summary: Opens the alef stanza, and the psalm, with a beatitude instead of a petition. The term is torah, teaching, and the claim is about conduct: blameless in the way, and walking.

stichs.en: Happy are those who keep His testimonies,
who seek Him with a whole heart.

verses.summary: The second beatitude narrows the first. Testimonies, edut, are what is kept, and the seeking is whole hearted, which brings in lev, heart, a word that runs through the whole stanza.

stichs.en: Indeed they have done no wrongdoing;
they have walked in His ways.

verses.summary: Stated first as a negative, then as a positive: nothing crooked done, His ways walked. The one verse of the stanza that names none of the eight terms for Torah, only two verbs of behaviour.

stichs.en: You Yourself have commanded Your precepts,
to be kept diligently.

verses.summary: The first direct address to God. Precepts, pikudim, appear for the first time, and the adverb me'od makes the keeping strict rather than approximate.

stichs.en: If only my ways were made firm,
to keep Your statutes.

verses.summary: The first wish in the psalm. Statutes, chukim, arrive here, and what is wished for is not divine action but that the speaker's own ways would hold steady.

stichs.en: Then I would not be ashamed,
when I look at all Your commandments.

verses.summary: Draws the consequence of the wish in verse 5. Commandments, mitzvot, and the condition attached is looking at all of them, not at a chosen few.

stichs.en: I will thank You with an upright heart,
when I learn Your righteous judgments.

verses.summary: A vow of thanks made conditional on study. The term is mishpatim, judgments, and learning them is what is expected to make the heart upright in the first place.

stichs.en: I will keep Your statutes;
do not abandon me utterly.

verses.summary: Closes the alef stanza by setting a promise beside a plea. Statutes again, and the first imperative the psalm addresses to God is a negative one: do not leave.

stichs.en: By what shall a young man keep his path pure?
By keeping it according to Your word.

verses.summary: Opens bet with the only real question in the slice, and answers it in the same breath. The term is davar, word, and the subject is a na'ar, a young man, not the speaker.

stichs.en: With all my heart I have sought You;
do not let me stray from Your commandments.

verses.summary: Takes the whole hearted seeking of verse 2 out of the third person and into the first, then adds what verse 2 did not have: a plea against going off course.

stichs.en: In my heart I have stored Your saying,
so that I would not sin against You.

verses.summary: The term is imrah, the spoken promise, and tzafanti is the verb used for hiding treasure away. The purpose clause states the aim without ornament: not to sin.

stichs.en: Blessed are You, LORD;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: A liturgical blessing formula drops into the acrostic, followed by a request of two words. Statutes, and lamdeni, teach me, which the psalm will ask again and again.

stichs.en: With my lips I have recounted
all the judgments of Your mouth.

verses.summary: The mirror of verse 11: what was stored inside the heart is now spoken out loud. Judgments, mishpatim, and they are located at Your mouth rather than in a book.

stichs.en: In the way of Your testimonies I have rejoiced,
as much as over all wealth.

verses.summary: Delight measured in money. Testimonies, and the comparison with all wealth is the first of several places where the psalm prices Torah against property.

stichs.en: On Your precepts let me meditate,
and let me look hard at Your paths.

verses.summary: Four words, the shortest verse in the slice, and both of its verbs are verbs of attention rather than action. Precepts paired with paths, thought paired with looking.

stichs.en: In Your statutes I will take delight;
I will not forget Your word.

verses.summary: Closes bet by putting two terms in one verse, statutes and word. The verb eshta'asha is reflexive and built on a root of play, so the delight is something done to oneself.

stichs.en: Deal generously with Your servant, that I may live,
and I will keep Your word.

verses.summary: Opens gimel by asking for bounty so that living itself becomes possible. Word, davar, and the keeping of it is offered back as the return on the gift.

stichs.en: Uncover my eyes,
that I may gaze at wonders out of Your teaching.

verses.summary: The plea is for sight, not for instruction. Torah is where the wonders already are, and gal, uncover, treats the obstacle as a covering over the reader rather than the text.

stichs.en: I am a resident alien on the earth;
do not hide Your commandments from me.

verses.summary: States the speaker's legal status: a ger, a stranger with no land. Commandments are what such a person most needs and could most easily be denied, hence the plea.

stichs.en: My soul is worn through with longing
for Your judgments at every moment.

verses.summary: Desire described as physical wear on the body. Judgments, mishpatim, and the phrase at every time makes the longing continuous rather than occasional.

stichs.en: You have rebuked the insolent, the accursed,
who stray from Your commandments.

verses.summary: The one verse of the stanza about other people. Straying from commandments is what makes the insolent accursed, and the rebuke is reported as something God has already done.

stichs.en: Roll scorn and contempt away from me,
for I have kept Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Uses gal again, the verb of verse 18, now for rolling shame off rather than uncovering eyes. Testimonies, and the plea rests on the claim that they were kept.

stichs.en: Even when princes sat and spoke against me,
Your servant kept meditating on Your statutes.

verses.summary: Eight words, the longest verse in the stanza, setting two scenes side by side: officials conspiring, and the speaker studying. No verb of complaint appears in either half.

stichs.en: Yes, Your testimonies are my delight,
the men of my counsel.

verses.summary: Closes gimel by calling testimonies both a delight and a body of advisers. Read against verse 23, the text replaces the princes as the counsel the speaker keeps.

stichs.en: My soul clings to the dust;
revive me according to Your word.

verses.summary: Opens dalet at ground level, the soul stuck to the dirt. Word, davar, and chayeni, revive me, which becomes the recurring imperative of this stanza.

stichs.en: I recounted my ways and You answered me;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: A conversation has already taken place: I told, You answered. The request that follows is word for word the request of verse 12, now made on the strength of that answer.

stichs.en: Make me understand the way of Your precepts,
and let me talk over Your wonders.

verses.summary: Understanding is asked for as the condition of speech, not as an end. Precepts, and the second verb is the asicha of verse 15, which covers both silent thought and talking.

stichs.en: My soul drips away from grief;
stand me up again according to Your word.

verses.summary: The soul that clung in verse 25 now leaks away. Word again, but the imperative changes from revive me to kaymeni, put me back on my feet.

stichs.en: Take the way of falsehood away from me,
and grace me with Your teaching.

verses.summary: The only petition in the stanza that asks for a removal. Falsehood is itself a derech, a way, and it is set against torah, which is asked for as a favour rather than earned.

stichs.en: The way of faithfulness I have chosen;
Your judgments I have set before me.

verses.summary: The counterpart of verse 29: a way chosen rather than a way removed, and the choice is the speaker's own. Judgments, and shiviti places them permanently in view.

stichs.en: I have clung to Your testimonies;
LORD, do not put me to shame.

verses.summary: Takes davak, the clinging verb of verse 25, off the dust and attaches it to testimonies. The plea against shame answers the confidence of verse 6 from the other side.

stichs.en: The way of Your commandments I will run,
for You widen my heart.

verses.summary: Closes dalet by moving from walking to running. Commandments, and the reason given for the speed is not resolve but a heart that God makes roomy.

stichs.en: Instruct me, LORD, in the way of Your statutes,
and I will guard it to the end.

verses.summary: Opens he, the stanza where every verse begins with an imperative aimed at God. Statutes, and ekev, a word for a heel or a consequence, is read here as right to the finish.

stichs.en: Give me understanding, and I will guard Your teaching,
and I will keep it with a whole heart.

verses.summary: Understanding requested as the means of observance rather than as knowledge for its own sake. Torah here, and the whole heart of verse 2 returns as the measure of keeping.

stichs.en: Walk me along the track of Your commandments,
for in it I take pleasure.

verses.summary: The request is to be walked, not for strength to walk. Commandments, and the ground given is desire rather than duty, which is unusual for a petition of this kind.

stichs.en: Bend my heart toward Your testimonies,
and not toward unjust gain.

verses.summary: Asks God to turn the will itself, not the circumstances. Testimonies are set against betza, profit taken unfairly, which is the sharpest of the psalm's rival objects of desire.

stichs.en: Turn my eyes away from seeing what is empty;
in Your ways revive me.

verses.summary: Eyes again, as in verse 18, but here to be turned away rather than uncovered. The first half names no term for Torah, only shav, emptiness, the thing not to be looked at.

stichs.en: Make Your promise stand for Your servant,
the promise that leads to fear of You.

verses.summary: Imrah, the promise, is what should be made to stand. The relative clause is grammatically hard and is read in more than one way: the promise either belongs to the fear of God or produces it.

stichs.en: Take away the reproach I dread,
for Your judgments are good.

verses.summary: Repeats the imperative of verse 37, now aimed at reproach instead of at the eyes. Judgments are called good, and their goodness is offered as the reason the reproach should go.

stichs.en: Look, I have longed for Your precepts;
by Your righteousness revive me.

verses.summary: Closes he with the one verse of the stanza that does not open on an imperative. Precepts, and the revival is grounded in God's righteousness rather than in the speaker's longing.

stichs.en: And let Your acts of kindness reach me, LORD,
Your rescue, as You promised.

glosses: and let them come to me
verses.summary: Opens vav, the stanza in which every verse begins with the conjunction and. What is asked for is kindness and rescue, and the yardstick given is imrah, the promise.

stichs.en: And I will have an answer for the one who taunts me,
for I have trusted in Your word.

verses.summary: States the purpose of the rescue asked for in verse 41: something to say back. Davar appears twice, once as the answer given and once as the word relied on.

stichs.en: And do not snatch the word of truth from my mouth,
not at all,
for I have waited for Your judgment.

verses.summary: Ten words, the longest verse in the slice. It continues the speech of verse 42 by asking that the true word not be taken out of the mouth, with judgment as the thing waited on.

stichs.en: And I will keep Your teaching continually,
forever and ever.

verses.summary: Answers verse 43 with a vow of permanence. Torah, and three separate time words stacked in five, so the sentence ends on duration rather than on content.

stichs.en: And let me walk about in open ground,
for I have sought out Your precepts.

verses.summary: Freedom is stated as a physical space. The cohortative asks for room to walk, and the ground given for it is that the speaker went looking for the precepts. Constraint and openness turn out to be the same thing.

stichs.en: And let me speak of Your testimonies before kings,
and I will not be ashamed.

verses.summary: The only verse in this stretch that puts the speaker in a royal court. Testimonies are the word chosen because they are meant to be said out loud, and the risk named is shame rather than danger.

stichs.en: And let me take delight in Your commandments,
which I have loved.

verses.summary: The verb is a reflexive of the root for play, and it will come back at 70 and 77. Commandments are loved here before they are obeyed, which reverses the expected order.

stichs.en: And let me lift my palms toward Your commandments, which I have loved,
and let me meditate on Your statutes.

verses.summary: A gesture of prayer redirected: the open hands go up toward the commandments rather than toward heaven. The second half drops from loving to studying, and the closing word of the vav stanza is statutes.

stichs.en: Remember the word to Your servant,
because You have made me hope.

verses.summary: Zayin opens by turning the psalm's own verb of memory back on God. The claim made is deliberately small: the hope being appealed to was God's doing in the first place.

stichs.en: This is my comfort in my affliction,
that Your promise has kept me alive.

verses.summary: The psalm's recurring plea, give me life, appears here in the past tense: it has already happened. Affliction is named before the comfort rather than after it.

stichs.en: The arrogant have mocked me to the utmost;
from Your Torah I have not turned aside.

verses.summary: The opposition finally gets a name, zedim, and it returns at 69, 78 and 85. Their weapon is ridicule, and the answer is a verb of geometry: no deviation from the line.

stichs.en: I have remembered Your judgments from of old,
O LORD, and I took comfort.

verses.summary: Old rulings, not new ones. Comfort is drawn from precedent here: what God has judged before is the evidence that the present case will be judged too.

stichs.en: Raging heat has seized me,
because of the wicked who abandon Your Torah.

verses.summary: A rare noun for burning rage, and it is aimed at people rather than at circumstances. The anger is on God's behalf, a different posture from the complaints elsewhere in the psalm.

stichs.en: Songs is what Your statutes have been to me,
in the house of my sojournings.

verses.summary: Statutes set to music. A house of sojournings is a traveller's temporary lodging, so the law becomes the thing carried rather than the thing left behind at home.

stichs.en: I have remembered Your name in the night, O LORD,
and I have kept Your Torah.

verses.summary: Night, when nothing can be checked and nothing performed for an audience. Remembering the Name is paired with keeping the Torah, so memory and practice are stated as one act.

stichs.en: This has been mine:
that I have guarded Your precepts.

verses.summary: The stanza closes by asking what the speaker actually owns. The answer is not a reward for keeping the precepts but the keeping itself, counted as the possession.

stichs.en: My portion is the LORD;
I have said that I would keep Your words.

verses.summary: Het opens in the language of land allotment. What the other tribes received as territory the speaker claims as God, and the vow that follows is to keep words rather than fields.

stichs.en: I have entreated Your face with all my heart;
be gracious to me according to Your promise.

verses.summary: The idiom is literally to soften someone's face. With all the heart is the psalm's measure of undivided attention, and it returns at 69 and 80.

stichs.en: I have reckoned up my ways,
and I turned my feet back toward Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Accounting first, then movement. The verb for turning back is the ordinary word for repentance, but its object here is the feet rather than the soul.

stichs.en: I hurried and I did not delay,
to keep Your commandments.

verses.summary: Speed treated as a form of obedience. Hurried and did not delay say the same thing twice, which in biblical Hebrew is emphasis rather than padding.

stichs.en: The cords of the wicked have encircled me;
Your Torah I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: Being tied up and not forgetting are simply set side by side. Nothing is requested in this verse: it reports only that memory survived the binding.

stichs.en: At the middle of the night I rise to give thanks to You,
for the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The night of verse 55 returns as a fixed hour. What the midnight rising is for is thanks rather than petition, and the grounds are the rightness of the rulings.

stichs.en: I am a companion to all who fear You,
and to those who keep Your precepts.

verses.summary: The one social verse in the stanza. Belonging is defined by practice and not by kinship: the company is whoever fears God and keeps the precepts, whoever that turns out to be.

stichs.en: Your kindness, O LORD, fills the earth;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The stanza widens to the whole earth and then narrows in two words to a single request. Teach me is the psalm's most frequent imperative, and kindness is what makes it askable.

stichs.en: You have dealt well with Your servant,
O LORD, according to Your word.

verses.summary: Tet opens with the word that starts five of its eight verses, good. The claim is retrospective, so the requests that follow in this stanza are not speculative.

stichs.en: Teach me good discernment and knowledge,
for I have believed in Your commandments.

verses.summary: What is asked for is not information but taste, the faculty of telling one thing from another. Belief in the commandments is offered as the qualification for receiving it.

stichs.en: Before I was afflicted I was straying,
but now I have kept Your promise.

verses.summary: The most exposed admission in the psalm: the straying stopped when the suffering started. Before and now split the verse in half, and the verb for erring is the one used of unintentional sin.

stichs.en: You are good and You do good;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: Good is turned from a description into an action by the third word, and the request rides straight off it. Five words, the shortest verse in this stretch.

stichs.en: The arrogant have smeared a lie against me;
I, with all my heart, will guard Your precepts.

verses.summary: The arrogant of verse 51 escalate from mockery to fabrication. With all the heart from verse 58 comes back as the counterweight to what they are smearing on.

stichs.en: Their heart has grown gross like fat;
I take delight in Your Torah.

verses.summary: Their heart against my delight. Fat here means insensible rather than rich, a heart too padded to feel anything, set opposite the play-verb of verse 47.

stichs.en: It is good for me that I was afflicted,
so that I might learn Your statutes.

verses.summary: Verse 67 reported what happened; this one calls it good. The affliction is reclassified as teaching, and the purpose clause names the syllabus it was for.

stichs.en: Better for me is the Torah of Your mouth
than thousands in gold and silver.

verses.summary: Torah of Your mouth, spoken rather than written, and the phrase returns in altered form at the end of the kaf stanza. The comparison is openly commercial: thousands in metal, and it still loses.

stichs.en: Your hands made me and set me firm;
give me understanding, and let me learn Your commandments.

verses.summary: Yod opens on the meaning of its own letter, hand. The argument runs from manufacture: whoever built the thing is the one asked to supply its understanding.

stichs.en: Those who fear You will see me and rejoice,
because I have hoped for Your word.

verses.summary: The speaker's rescue is offered as public evidence. Others who fear God are watching, and what gladdens them is that hoping in the word turned out to be justified.

stichs.en: I know, O LORD, that Your judgments are righteous,
and that in faithfulness You afflicted me.

verses.summary: The hardest sentence in the psalm. The affliction of 67 and 71 is not explained away but attributed, and attributed to faithfulness rather than to anger.

stichs.en: Let Your kindness, please, be there to comfort me,
according to Your promise to Your servant.

verses.summary: The first please in this stretch. Kindness is assigned one specific job, comforting, and the grounds are a promise already made to a servant rather than a fresh claim.

stichs.en: Let Your mercies come to me, and let me live,
for Your Torah is my delight.

verses.summary: Mercies in the plural, from the word for womb, asked to arrive so that living can resume. The delight of 47 and 70 returns here as the reason rather than the response.

stichs.en: Let the arrogant be ashamed, for with falsehood they have wronged me;
I will meditate on Your precepts.

verses.summary: The one curse in the stanza, and it is minimal: let them be ashamed, nothing worse than that. The speaker's own response is to go on turning the precepts over to himself.

stichs.en: Let those who fear You turn back to me,
and those who know Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Turning of a different kind from verse 59: here it is other people asked to turn back toward the speaker. Standing among the faithful is treated as something worth praying for.

stichs.en: Let my heart be whole in Your statutes,
so that I will not be ashamed.

verses.summary: Yod closes with the shame of verse 78 turned inward. Tamim, unblemished, is a word from the sacrifice laws applied to a heart, and the statutes are where that wholeness gets measured.

stichs.en: My soul has worn itself out for Your deliverance;
for Your word I have hoped.

verses.summary: Kaf opens with a verb of exhaustion that governs its first two verses. The soul is spent and the last two words still say hope, which is the tension the whole stanza runs on.

stichs.en: My eyes have worn out for Your promise,
saying: when will You comfort me?

verses.summary: The same exhaustion verb as 81, now with the eyes as its subject rather than the soul. Here alone the speaker quotes his own question back, and it is a question about timing.

stichs.en: For I have become like a skin bottle in the smoke;
Your statutes I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: A leather bottle hung over a fire until it shrivels and cracks. The image is of drying out rather than of burning, and it is answered by the flattest claim available: not forgotten.

stichs.en: How many are the days of Your servant?
When will You execute judgment on my pursuers?

verses.summary: Two questions with no statement between them. This is the only verse in the stretch that asks God to act against anyone, and it makes the ask by way of the speaker's own lifespan.

stichs.en: The arrogant have dug pits for me,
which is not according to Your Torah.

verses.summary: The arrogant move from words to earthworks. The relative clause carries the weight: digging pits is measured against the Torah and found to fall outside it.

stichs.en: All Your commandments are faithfulness;
with falsehood they have pursued me; help me.

verses.summary: Faithfulness is asserted of the commandments and falsehood of the pursuers, the two nouns set directly against each other. The verse ends on a single word of appeal.

stichs.en: They almost finished me off in the land,
but I have not abandoned Your precepts.

verses.summary: Almost is the whole verse. The near-killing is reported in three words and answered by four, and the answer is not a rescue but a record of what was not let go.

stichs.en: According to Your kindness give me life,
and let me keep the testimony of Your mouth.

verses.summary: The stanza ends where 50 began, with give me life, now as a request instead of a report. Testimony of Your mouth answers Torah of Your mouth at 72, closing the two halves of this slice on the same phrase.

stichs.en: Forever, LORD,
Your word stands firm in the heavens.

verses.summary: Lamed opens with davar, the word, and with no request at all. The claim is that the word is already fixed in heaven, older than the speaker's need of it.

stichs.en: To generation after generation is Your faithfulness;
You established the earth, and it stands.

verses.summary: One of the two verses in the psalm that use none of the eight Torah words. Faithfulness stands in their place, and the proof offered is the earth, which was set up and simply keeps standing.

stichs.en: By Your judgments they stand today,
for everything is Your servant.

verses.summary: Mishpatim, the judgments, read cosmically. The same rulings that govern the speaker hold the day in place, and every created thing is enrolled as a servant.

stichs.en: Had Your teaching not been my delight,
I would then have perished in my affliction.

verses.summary: The first counterfactual of the stanza. Torah is called sha'ashua, delight, and the claim is bare survival: without that delight the affliction would already have finished him.

stichs.en: Never will I forget Your precepts,
for through them You have kept me alive.

verses.summary: Pikudim, precepts, joined to a promise never to forget. The reason arrives in a single word, through them, which credits the precepts themselves with keeping him alive.

stichs.en: I am Yours, save me,
for I have sought Your precepts.

verses.summary: The shortest possession claim in the psalm: I am Yours. The imperative hoshieni, save me, rests on that ownership and on the fact that he went looking for the pikudim.

stichs.en: The wicked have lain in wait for me to destroy me;
I study Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Two parties wait at once. They wait to destroy, and while they wait he studies the edot, so the ambush is answered by attention rather than by flight.

stichs.en: To all perfection I have seen an end;
Your commandment is exceedingly broad.

verses.summary: The one verse here that measures Torah against everything else. He has found a limit to all completeness; only the mitzvah is called broad, and exceedingly is the last word of the stanza.

stichs.en: How I love Your teaching!
All the day it is my meditation.

verses.summary: Mem opens with an exclamation, not a petition. Torah is loved and named sichah, the thing he talks over all day, which sets up the three comparisons that follow.

stichs.en: Wiser than my enemies Your commandments make me,
for they are mine forever.

verses.summary: First of three comparisons: wiser than enemies. The mitzvot are the instrument, and the singular pronoun treats them as one possession that never leaves him.

stichs.en: More than all my teachers I have grown wise,
for Your testimonies are my meditation.

verses.summary: Second comparison, and the risky one: more insight than his teachers. The edot are what he keeps talking over, so the claim is about attention, not native talent.

stichs.en: More than elders I understand,
because I have kept Your precepts.

verses.summary: Third comparison, the elders, and here the reason shifts from meditation to conduct: he understands because he has guarded the pikudim, not because he has thought harder.

stichs.en: From every evil path I have held back my feet,
so that I may keep Your word.

verses.summary: A negative discipline. Feet held back from every evil path, with lema'an, in order that, making the restraint purposeful: it exists so the davar can be kept.

stichs.en: From Your judgments I have not turned aside,
for You Yourself have taught me.

verses.summary: The paired negative: no turning aside from the mishpatim. The reason is handed to God as teacher, so standing still is not counted as the speaker's own achievement.

stichs.en: How smooth to my palate is Your saying,
sweeter than honey to my mouth.

verses.summary: The taste verse. Imrah, the saying, is placed on the palate and rated against honey, the only place in this stretch where Torah is measured by a sense rather than an argument.

stichs.en: From Your precepts I gain understanding;
therefore I hate every false path.

verses.summary: Mem closes the way it argued. Understanding comes out of the pikudim, and that understanding produces hatred of every false path, so knowledge here has a moral edge and not only a scope.

stichs.en: A lamp for my foot is Your word,
and a light for my path.

verses.summary: Nun opens with the most quoted line of the psalm. Davar as a lamp is small, local light, enough for one step, which is exactly what a foot needs.

stichs.en: I have sworn, and I will fulfill it,
to keep the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: A verse of oath. The unusual doubling, sworn and then confirmed, binds him twice over to the mishpatim, which are named here as the judgments of Your righteousness.

stichs.en: I am afflicted very much;
LORD, give me life according to Your word.

verses.summary: The first plain complaint of the stanza. Affliction is stated with no cause given, and the request chayeni, give me life, is measured strictly by the davar.

stichs.en: Accept, please, the freewill offerings of my mouth, LORD,
and teach me Your judgments.

verses.summary: Sacrificial language borrowed for speech: what he brings are the freewill offerings of his mouth. The second half asks for instruction in the mishpatim, so praise and learning arrive in one breath.

stichs.en: My soul is in my palm continually,
yet Your teaching I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: Life carried in the palm is an idiom for constant danger. The counterweight is memory: even so, the torah has not been forgotten, and that contrast is the whole line.

stichs.en: The wicked have set a trap for me,
yet from Your precepts I have not strayed.

verses.summary: The danger of verse 109 becomes concrete, a trap laid by the wicked. The answering verb is not escape but not straying from the pikudim, so staying on course is the survival move.

stichs.en: I have taken Your testimonies as my inheritance forever,
for they are the joy of my heart.

verses.summary: The vocabulary turns legal. The edot are taken as a nachalah, an inherited holding rather than a duty, and the reason given for wanting it is joy.

stichs.en: I have inclined my heart to do Your statutes,
forever, to the very end.

verses.summary: Nun closes on an act of will: the heart bent toward doing the chukim. The last word fixes the term, all the way to the end, giving the stanza a horizon rather than a mood.

stichs.en: The divided I hate,
but Your teaching I love.

verses.summary: Samech opens on a hated object, the divided or half hearted, set directly opposite love of the torah. Four words, two verbs, and the stanza's theme of separation is already set.

stichs.en: My hiding place and my shield are You;
for Your word I wait.

verses.summary: Two shelter nouns, then a verb of waiting. Nothing is actually requested: the davar is what he waits on, and the waiting is offered as the response to danger.

stichs.en: Turn away from me, you evildoers,
that I may keep the commandments of my God.

verses.summary: The rare imperative addressed to people rather than to God. Evildoers are told to leave, and the stated purpose is keeping the mitzvot, so company is treated as an obstacle to practice.

stichs.en: Uphold me according to Your saying, that I may live,
and do not let me be shamed of my hope.

verses.summary: Two requests fused into one: hold me up by the imrah so that I live, and do not let my hope be disgraced. Living and not being shamed are asked for as the same favour.

stichs.en: Support me, that I may be saved,
and I will gaze on Your statutes continually.

verses.summary: Rescue asked for with a purpose clause attached. Held upright, he can keep looking at the chukim without stopping, so being saved is wanted in order that study can continue.

stichs.en: You have set aside all who stray from Your statutes,
for their deceit is falsehood.

verses.summary: The judgment half of the stanza. Those who wander from the chukim are set aside, and the reason given is that their cleverness is a lie, not that they are weak.

stichs.en: Like dross You have removed all the wicked of the earth;
therefore I love Your testimonies.

verses.summary: A metallurgical image: the wicked skimmed off like the scum on molten metal. The speaker draws his own conclusion from it, love of the edot, so the verse ends with him and not with them.

stichs.en: My flesh bristles in dread of You,
and of Your judgments I am afraid.

verses.summary: Samech ends in the body. Flesh bristles, and the object of the dread is the mishpatim themselves, which turns the judgment of verse 118 back onto the speaker.

stichs.en: I have done justice and righteousness;
do not leave me to my oppressors.

verses.summary: Ayin opens with a claim of merit, rare in this psalm. Having done mishpat himself, all he asks is not to be handed over to those pressing him.

stichs.en: Stand surety for Your servant for good;
let the arrogant not oppress me.

verses.summary: The second of the two verses using none of the eight Torah words. It asks God to act as guarantor for His own servant, a term taken from debt law rather than from Torah.

stichs.en: My eyes have failed for Your salvation,
and for the saying of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: Eyes giving out is the idiom for waiting past endurance. Two things are awaited at once, the salvation and the imrah, which makes rescue and word a single expected arrival.

stichs.en: Deal with Your servant according to Your kindness,
and teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The measure named for the request is chesed, kindness, not the record claimed back in verse 121. What that kindness is asked to buy is instruction in the chukim.

stichs.en: I am Your servant, give me understanding,
that I may know Your testimonies.

verses.summary: The servant title of verse 122 turned into leverage for a request. Understanding is asked for with an explicit purpose attached: so that the edot can be known.

stichs.en: It is time to act for the LORD;
they have broken Your teaching.

verses.summary: The one verse in this stretch that speaks of God in the third person, and it tells Him when to move. The ground offered is that people have annulled the torah.

stichs.en: Therefore I love Your commandments
more than gold, more than fine gold.

verses.summary: The gold comparison. Mitzvot outrank both zahav and paz, the ordinary metal and the refined one, which is the only economic measure the ayin stanza uses.

stichs.en: Therefore all the precepts of everything I hold to be right;
every false path I hate.

verses.summary: The most emphatic verse of the stanza, with kol, all, appearing three times in ten words. Every one of the pikudim is declared straight, and the matching move is hatred of every false path.

stichs.en: Wonders are Your testimonies;
therefore my soul has kept them.

verses.summary: Pe opens by calling the edot wonders, the vocabulary of miracle rather than of law. What follows is guarding, and the guardian named is the nefesh itself.

stichs.en: The opening of Your words gives light,
giving understanding to the simple.

verses.summary: The teaching verse. What gives light is the petach, the opening or unfolding of the words, and the beneficiaries named are the simple rather than the learned.

stichs.en: I opened my mouth wide and panted,
for I longed for Your commandments.

verses.summary: A physical image of appetite, the mouth wide and the breath short. The object of the craving is the mitzvot, so desire and not duty is given as the reason for keeping them.

stichs.en: Turn to me and be gracious to me,
as is the rule for those who love Your name.

verses.summary: The turn to face. Two imperatives, turn and show favour, and the standard invoked is mishpat in its sense of customary practice, what is owed to those who love the Name.

stichs.en: Make my steps firm by Your word,
and let no iniquity rule over me.

verses.summary: Two requests in one breath, and they pull in opposite directions: hold the feet steady, and hold something else back. The Torah word is imrah, the spoken promise, used here as the ground underfoot rather than as something studied.

stichs.en: Redeem me from the oppression of man,
and I will keep Your precepts.

verses.summary: The pressure named in the previous verse was iniquity from within; here it is a human hand from outside. The consequence clause is the same shape both times: rescue first, then keeping. This one uses piqqudim.

stichs.en: Make Your face shine upon Your servant,
and teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: Light and instruction asked for as one thing. The vocabulary of the first half is the vocabulary of the priestly blessing; the second half turns that light into a lesson, and the word is chuqqim.

stichs.en: Streams of water run down from my eyes,
because they have not kept Your teaching.

verses.summary: The subject of the failing verb is an unnamed they, never identified. The weeping is not over the speaker's own trouble, which is what makes this verse unusual in a psalm otherwise spoken in the first person. Torah.

stichs.en: You are righteous, O LORD,
and Your judgments are upright.

verses.summary: The tzade stanza opens by conceding the verdict before any request is made. Both halves are verbless clauses, an adjective set beside a noun, which is how Hebrew states what simply is the case. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: You have commanded Your testimonies in righteousness,
and in great faithfulness.

verses.summary: The testimonies are not described here, they are commanded: the verb makes them an act performed rather than a document held. Righteousness and faithfulness are the manner of the commanding, not properties of the text. Edot.

stichs.en: My zeal has consumed me,
because my foes have forgotten Your words.

verses.summary: The damage is self-inflicted and the cause is other people. Zeal is the subject of the verb and the speaker is its object, which is a precise way of saying that caring about this is costing him. Devarim.

stichs.en: Your word is refined through and through,
and Your servant loves it.

verses.summary: The image is metallurgical: the participle is what is done to silver in a crucible. The love in the second half follows from the testing, not from sentiment. The suffix on the last verb is feminine, agreeing with imrah.

stichs.en: I am small and despised,
yet I have not forgotten Your precepts.

verses.summary: Social standing on one side, memory on the other, joined without any word for yet: the contrast is carried by juxtaposition alone. The same denial of forgetting will close the whole psalm. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: Your righteousness is righteousness forever,
and Your teaching is truth.

verses.summary: Four nouns and no verb in the entire verse. Nothing is claimed about what Torah does; two identities are asserted and left standing. Torah, paired with the abstract noun for truth.

stichs.en: Distress and anguish have found me,
yet Your commandments are my delight.

verses.summary: The tzade sounds crowd together in the first half, three words in a row built on the same consonant, so the line sounds pinched before it says it is. The word for delight returns at verse 174. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: Your testimonies are righteous forever;
give me understanding, that I may live.

verses.summary: The stanza ends by turning its own statement into a demand. What is true forever is no use until it is understood, and understanding is set as the condition of living, not its reward. Edot.

stichs.en: I have called with my whole heart;
answer me, O LORD;
I will keep Your statutes.

verses.summary: The qof stanza is built on the root for calling and the root for drawing near, and this is the first of two consecutive verses whose opening verb is a call. Note that the object comes before its verb in the last two words. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: I have called You: save me,
and I will keep Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Four words, one of the four shortest verses in the psalm. The object suffix on the first verb means the call is already addressed before anything is asked for. Edot, and the same promise clause as verse 134.

stichs.en: I was up before dawn and cried out;
I have hoped in Your word.

verses.summary: The verb does not mean to rise early, it means to get ahead of something, and what is outrun here is the daybreak. This is the only time stamp in the stanza. Davar.

stichs.en: My eyes got ahead of the night watches,
to meditate on Your word.

verses.summary: The same verb as the previous verse, now with the eyes as its subject rather than the whole person. The purpose is given by an infinitive, which is rare here: most verses state a promise instead. Imrah.

stichs.en: Hear my voice according to Your kindness, O LORD;
according to Your justice, revive me.

verses.summary: Two matched ke- prefixes set the measure of the request, first covenant kindness and then legal judgment, as if either standard would do. Revive me runs four times through this last quarter of the psalm. Mishpat.

stichs.en: Those who chase after scheming have drawn near;
they are far from Your teaching.

verses.summary: Near and far in one line, and the two verbs sit at opposite ends of the verse so the distance is visible on the page. This sets the trap the next verse springs. Torah.

stichs.en: You are near, O LORD,
and all Your commandments are truth.

verses.summary: The answer to the previous verse reuses its adjective: the pursuers are near, and so is God, and the psalm lets the two nearnesses stand side by side without ranking them. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: Long ago I learned from Your testimonies
that You founded them forever.

verses.summary: The testimonies are the source of the knowledge and also its object, so the claim is self-supporting by design. The closing verb is the one used for laying a foundation. Edot.

stichs.en: See my affliction and rescue me,
for I have not forgotten Your teaching.

verses.summary: The resh stanza opens with an imperative of looking, and the same imperative opens verse 159, bracketing the stanza. The ground offered is memory rather than merit. Torah.

stichs.en: Argue my case and redeem me;
revive me according to Your word.

verses.summary: A verb and its own noun stacked together, the construction Hebrew uses to say plead the plea. The vocabulary is a lawsuit in the first half and a family redeemer in the second. Imrah, first of three groundings for revive me in this stanza.

stichs.en: Salvation is far from the wicked,
for they have not sought Your statutes.

verses.summary: The far and near pairing from verse 150 returns, now applied to rescue rather than to people. The distance is presented as a consequence of not seeking, not as a punishment imposed. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: Your compassions are many, O LORD;
revive me according to Your judgments.

verses.summary: Second of the three revive me requests in this stanza, and each one names a different measure: word here becomes judgments, and will become kindness at verse 159. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: My pursuers and my foes are many,
yet I have not turned aside from Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Many is the first word of this verse and the second word of the last one, so mercies and persecutors are counted with the same adjective. The verb is spatial: not turning off a road. Edot.

stichs.en: I saw traitors and I contended with them,
because they did not keep Your word.

verses.summary: The middle verb is rare and its force is disputed: translations divide between quarrelling with them and being sickened by them. Either way the reaction is provoked by watching, not by being harmed. Imrah.

stichs.en: See how I love Your precepts;
O LORD, revive me according to Your kindness.

verses.summary: The look demanded at verse 153 is demanded again, closing the stanza, but now what is to be looked at is affection rather than affliction. Third revive me, this one measured by chesed. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: The sum of Your word is truth,
and every judgment of Your righteousness stands forever.

verses.summary: The first noun means head, and readers split over whether it points to the beginning of the word or to its total. Both readings are defended; the psalm does not settle it. Davar closing a stanza that began with Torah.

stichs.en: Princes have hunted me without cause,
but my heart dreads Your word.

verses.summary: The stanza opens by moving fear off its obvious target. Powerful men are chasing him and the thing his heart shakes at is a word. Davar, with the prefix meaning at or because of.

stichs.en: I rejoice over Your word
like one who finds great spoil.

verses.summary: The only simile in this stretch of the psalm, and it is taken from the battlefield: plunder found after the fighting, not wages earned. Great returns as the first adjective of verse 165. Imrah.

stichs.en: Falsehood I hate and abhor;
Your teaching I love.

verses.summary: Both halves put the object first and the verb second, so the sentence turns on the pivot between two hate verbs and one love verb. Nothing is asked for in this verse. Torah.

stichs.en: Seven times a day I have praised You,
for the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The only counted quantity in the stanza, and the number has been read both as a literal tally and as a round figure for completeness. The last two words are a chain of two nouns, judgments belonging to righteousness. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: Great peace belongs to those who love Your teaching,
and nothing makes them stumble.

verses.summary: The word for them here is an archaic poetic form, not the ordinary one, which is part of why this line reads as a formula rather than a report. The noun for stumbling block occurs only here in the psalm. Torah.

stichs.en: I have waited for Your salvation, O LORD,
and I have done Your commandments.

verses.summary: Waiting and acting reported in the same tense, side by side, with no suggestion that one is preparation for the other. The verb for hoping is uncommon. Mitzvot.

stichs.en: My soul has kept Your testimonies,
and I love them very much.

verses.summary: The keeping is credited to the nefesh rather than to the speaker, which puts the obedience below the level of decision. The plural object suffix on the love verb points back to the testimonies. Edot.

stichs.en: I have kept Your precepts and Your testimonies,
for all my ways are in front of You.

verses.summary: Two of the eight Torah words share one clause here, piqqudim and edot joined by a conjunction rather than split across the two halves. The reason given for obeying is being watched, not being rewarded.

stichs.en: Let my cry come near before You, O LORD;
give me understanding according to Your word.

verses.summary: The tav stanza is almost entirely jussive: let this happen, let that happen. The verb for drawing near is the one from the qof stanza, now applied to the speaker's own shout. Davar.

stichs.en: Let my plea come before You;
deliver me according to Your word.

verses.summary: Built on the same frame as the verse before it, with imrah swapped in for davar and rescue asked for instead of understanding. The pairing of the two synonyms across adjacent verses is deliberate.

stichs.en: Let my lips pour out praise,
for You teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The opening verb is used of a spring bubbling up, so the praise is asked for as something involuntary. Teaching is stated as ongoing rather than requested. Chuqqim.

stichs.en: Let my tongue answer with Your word,
for all Your commandments are righteousness.

verses.summary: The verb can mean answer or sing out, and both senses are in play here. Lips in the previous verse, tongue in this one: the organs of speech are asked for one at a time. Imrah and mitzvot in the same verse.

stichs.en: Let Your hand be there to help me,
for I have chosen Your precepts.

verses.summary: The ground offered is an act of will, and the verb for choosing appears only twice in the whole psalm, here and at verse 30. Everywhere else the speaker pleads memory or love instead. Piqqudim.

stichs.en: I have longed for Your salvation, O LORD,
and Your teaching is my delight.

verses.summary: Salvation echoes verse 166 and delight echoes verse 143, so the last stanza is gathering its own earlier vocabulary. Longing is stated as a completed act. Torah.

stichs.en: Let my soul live, and let it praise You,
and let Your judgments help me.

verses.summary: Living is asked for with a purpose attached, which is unusual: the request is not to survive but to be able to say something. In the second half the judgments become the agents of the help. Mishpatim.

stichs.en: I have strayed like a lost sheep;
seek out Your servant,
for I have not forgotten Your commandments.

verses.summary: One hundred and seventy five verses of keeping, and the last one admits to being lost. The imperative asks God to do the searching, and the final clause is the same denial of forgetting used at verses 141 and 153. Mitzvot.

pardes.body: Twenty two stanzas of eight verses. Inside a stanza every verse begins with the same letter: eight verses on alef, then eight on bet, through to eight on tav. Checked against this text the pattern holds in all twenty two stanzas without a single exception, so it is the skeleton of the poem rather than an ornament on it. There is no narrative. Nobody is rescued, no enemy is named, nothing is settled between the first verse and the last, and the psalm ends with the speaker still lost: {{176.0}}, I have strayed. What moves is not a plot but a position, restated 176 times under pressure. The unit to read is the block of eight, not the single verse.

Eight nouns carry the whole psalm: instruction {{34.2}}, testimonies {{14.1}}, precepts {{27.1}}, statutes {{5.4}}, commandments {{6.6}}, judgments {{20.4}}, word {{16.4}}, saying {{11.2}}. It is often said that one of the eight appears in every verse. Counted against this text the claim is close but not exact: 172 of the 176 verses carry at least one, 166 carry exactly one, six carry two, and four carry none. Verses 3 and 37 fill the slot with a ninth word, way, {{3.4}} and {{37.4}}. Verses 90 and 122 have nothing of the kind. Whether the eight are real synonyms is argued. The roots pull apart, statutes from engraving, precepts from appointing, judgments from judging, testimonies from witness, while the psalm uses them interchangeably often enough that many readers treat them as one word with eight faces.

Read it as a list of requests and the picture sharpens. The most repeated is not for knowledge but for life: {{25.3}}, keep me alive, nine times. Teach me, {{12.3}}, eight times. Give me understanding, six. Open my eyes, {{18.0}}, once, and that one is the sharpest, because it assumes the text is already in front of him and locates the failure in the seeing. Taken together the petitions read less like praise of the law from someone who has mastered it and more like the working prayer of someone studying it badly and in trouble. The custom of reciting the stanzas that spell a mourner's name, then the four letters of neshamah, uses the alphabet the same way: something you walk through, not something you admire.

The letters are the material, not the label. In the kabbalistic reading the twenty two letters are what the world is made of, so spending all of them, eight verses each, on a single subject is a statement about scope rather than a memory aid: whatever the letters can build, this is what it is for. Eight is the number just past a finished seven, the day after the full week, and it is the size of every stanza here. The tav stanza then closes not on arrival but on {{176.0}}, straying, and asks to be searched for. The alphabet is complete and the speaker is not, which is the point.
